claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch in an otherwise comparable high-entropy alloy enhances local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions impede dislocation motion by increasing nanoscale segment detrapping barriers.
Greater atomic size mismatch produces higher hardness than minimal atomic size mismatch.
Greater atomic size mismatch produces higher yield strength than minimal atomic size mismatch.
The proposed comparison is restricted to single-phase, disordered solid-solution alloys with similar grain size and minimal second-phase precipitation.
Replacing a principal element with a chemically similar element having a substantially different atomic radius will systematically increase local lattice distortion.
The proposed behavior applies under ambient to moderately elevated temperatures and strain rates where dislocation glide dominates plasticity.
In high-entropy alloys, dislocation motion can be governed by nanoscale segment detrapping from local energy barriers.
Increasing barriers to dislocation movement elevates yield strength.
Increasing barriers to dislocation movement elevates hardness.
Minimizing atomic size differences among constituent elements produces lower local lattice distortion.
The proposed relationship may fail when grain-boundary effects or phase transformations dominate deformation.
The magnitude of strengthening may vary with alloy system, processing history, and testing conditions.
Failure of the increased-mismatch alloy to show consistently higher yield strength and hardness would falsify the proposed directional relationship.

contradictions.description: The design calls the two alloys identical in overall composition while also requiring substitution of one principal element. Elemental substitution necessarily changes composition; the intended control is presumably identical processing and matched microstructure rather than identical overall composition.
